entries.body: Pressing the count of existing conversations beside a paragraph started a new empty one instead of opening any of them, and quietly added another to the count each time. It now opens the conversation about that paragraph, and a separate button starts a new one.

entries.title: Add a linked article to your library
entries.body: Point at a link in an article and the card that appears carries an Add to Spideryarn button. It starts adding that page to your library there and then, without opening a new tab or taking you out of the piece you are reading. Your library picks the article up once it has finished being added, even if you have moved on and the card has closed.

entries.title: Shared articles and their details look right
entries.body: The notice at the top of a shared article was drawn as a flat panel rather than a raised one with a border, and on a public article's details the built and not-built rows were all the same grey. Those, and some of the text that appears when you point at something, look right again.

entries.title: Fewer controls above the article
entries.body: The controls above the article are down to what you use: the switch for the strip that shows where you are has gone, and the layout decides when to show it; so have the argument-level button in Hierarchy and the keyboard readout. Hierarchy's column labels are hidden to save vertical space, and the panel beside the article no longer repeats its own name at the top. The mode you are in is named on the bar at the bottom instead, including while that panel is open.

entries.title: Short selections can be commented on
entries.body: Selecting a short phrase, like AI or GDP, used to do nothing, or open a comment left on a different passage. A selection of two characters or more now opens the comment option on exactly the words you picked.

entries.title: Debate mode shows published responses to an article
entries.body: Debate gathers pages published in response to an article you have added, grouped and marked for whether they agree or disagree, with the passages each one quotes. A page is listed only when it names the article, so an unrelated page cannot appear as a response to it, and when nothing is found it says so rather than leaving you guessing. It is behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: A section's question replaces its one-line summary
entries.body: Where the app has written a question about a section, the Summary panel shows that question on its own line, in place of the short summary. Before, the question sat underneath in smaller italics, which made a real question look like a footnote.

entries.title: Library controls are the same on every article
entries.body: The same five controls appear on every article in your library, in both the card and the compact list view, rather than on some and not others. Pointing at one says what it does, and why it is unavailable when it is. Refreshing is offered only for articles that came from a web address.

entries.title: Quotes finds more lines and marks them all
entries.body: Quotes asks for about twice as many lines from an article as it did, and every quotation in the list is marked in the text itself, not only the one you have selected. It also allows longer to gather them, and offers to redo a list drawn up under the old settings.

entries.title: A deleted article no longer comes back
entries.body: The app keeps a copy of your library on your device so it can show it quickly. If a request was still on its way back when you deleted something, the older reply could win and the deleted item would reappear. The order is respected now, and signing out or making a change clears what was kept.

entries.title: Quizzes start with easier questions
entries.body: Questions written from an article start easier, and draw on the material the piece leans on rather than its edges. Quizzes made under the old settings are marked as out of date, so you can have one written again.

entries.title: Feedback stops repeating your email address
entries.body: The Feedback form no longer shows your email address back to you. If a report cannot be sent, the message it offers to open instead is addressed to our public contact address.

entries.title: Links show where they lead, and why
entries.body: Point at a link in an article and a card shows the page it leads to — its title and its opening description. Below that, a short paragraph says why the link is there and how it bears on the passage you are reading; it appears as it is written. A link you have already looked at does not have to be worked out a second time.

entries.title: Remember mode has a new icon
entries.body: Remember mode's button in the row of modes is a brain rather than a speech bubble, so it is easier to tell apart from Chat beside it.

entries.title: Glossary, Quotes and Debate work again
entries.body: On some articles, asking for anything new — a glossary, the quotes, a debate — failed every time, and the message suggested that trying again was worth a go. It was not. Those articles can make all of it again.

entries.title: Answers that stop early are no longer accepted
entries.body: If the AI stopped partway through, its half-answer could be shown as a finished one — in Chat, Referee, Search, explanations and quiz marking. It is reported as cut short instead. A complete answer that landed just as the time limit ran out could also be thrown away as a timeout; it is kept.

entries.title: Library buttons explain before they act
entries.body: On a touch screen, tapping an action in your library both explained what it does and did it at once. The first tap shows the explanation and the second carries it out, as elsewhere in the app. Copy link also tells you when the browser will not give it the clipboard.

entries.title: Link previews match the link you point at
entries.body: When an article links to the same page twice, pointing at the second link showed a summary written about the first link's paragraph. Each link now gives a summary of the passage it sits in. Links outside the article text — in chat answers or a figure view — show the ordinary preview of the destination, without that article summary.

entries.title: Shorter top-level summaries, fuller ones up close
entries.body: The one-sentence summary of a whole article is shorter than it was, and the summaries of smaller sections carry more detail, so zooming in tells you more rather than less. They also avoid describing the order the piece is written in. Articles you add from here on use the new wording; older summaries change when they are generated again.

entries.title: A fault in Ideas stays inside Ideas
entries.body: If something goes wrong while Ideas is drawing, only that panel is replaced by a message; the article, the strip showing where you are, and the bar at the bottom keep working. A button you pressed just before the failure is discarded too, so it cannot fire later when you go back.

entries.title: A bad answer no longer loses the summaries
entries.body: When the app builds an article's levels of detail, an answer from the AI could arrive slightly malformed and the whole thing was thrown away, so the summaries failed or had to be tried again. Those answers are read correctly now.

entries.title: Keyboard focus follows the drawer and comments
entries.body: Opening the drawer at the bottom of the article moves the keyboard cursor into it, and closing it returns the cursor to where you were. Opening a comment, switching to another, or deleting the last one leaves focus somewhere sensible rather than nowhere. It also no longer tells a screen reader that the page behind it is blocked.

entries.title: Figures from PDFs appear in the article
entries.body: When you add a paper as a PDF, its pictures now show in the text beside their captions, for you and for anyone you share the article with. Where a figure could not be recovered you get a short note saying so, instead of a blank space or a broken image. On your own articles, each figure also links to that page of the original PDF.

entries.title: Diagram, Quiz and Referee start on one press
entries.body: On an article you own, pressing Diagram now draws the picture rather than waiting for a second press. The same goes for Tweets on the article bar, the Quiz chip in Remember, and the Claims and Candidates chips in Referee; arriving from a pasted link or the Back button still waits for you to ask. Referee also shows its note about the search engine it uses before Candidates runs.

entries.title: Quotes is on the bar for everyone
entries.body: Quotes, which gathers the lines in a piece worth keeping, is no longer behind the Experimental features switch. It sits on the mode bar for every reader and runs the first time you press it, as Glossary and Ideas do. Timeline, Referee, Remember and Debate are still behind the switch on your profile page.

entries.title: An article says where it came from
entries.body: The web address an article came from now sits directly under its title, with the site name to the fore and the rest faded. On your own articles, one that came from an uploaded file says so, as does one with no address recorded. The tips about origin and sharing are now the app's fuller cards.

entries.title: Debate stops doubting sources that name the piece
entries.body: In Debate, a source that did name the article could be marked as unverified when the title's punctuation differed — a curly apostrophe against a straight one. Both spellings are now read as the same, so an on-topic citation is recognised. Debate is behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: Spoken conversation shows what it is doing
entries.body: The spoken conversation in Chat shows what it is doing: which microphone it is using and whether it can hear you, a running transcript, and whether it is listening, thinking or speaking. You can cancel while it connects, retry after a failure, hang up, or switch to typing or dictating instead. A conversation you come back to is kept, along with answers that were cut off, and if your browser blocks the sound there is a button to turn it on.

entries.title: Logo and Feedback moved into the controls bar
entries.body: The Spideryarn logo no longer floats in the corner, and Feedback no longer sits opposite it; both are in the row of controls at the bottom, Feedback when you are signed in. On a phone the logo had been swallowing taps meant for the strip that shows where you are, and titles now line up with the text.

entries.title: Footer points to Contact rather than an email
entries.body: The email address has gone from the row at the bottom of every page. The Contact link is still there and still carries the address, along with the Feedback button.

entries.title: Controls row no longer overflows when switching modes
entries.body: Switching mode could reveal the name of the mode you had picked and push the row of controls wider than the window. The row is measured again when you switch, so it fits.

entries.title: Jump back to where you came from
entries.body: Following a glossary term or a footnote can land you thousands of words from where you were. A chip now names the place you jumped from and takes you back to it, and the strip showing where you are marks the spot you left. It works where the browser's Back button does not, such as the app installed to your home screen. Opening a question that is already on the screen no longer offers to take you back to a place you never left.

entries.title: Upload an HTML file, not just a PDF
entries.body: You can add an article by uploading an HTML file as well as a PDF. When a page or a PDF cannot be read properly — too little text, or pages that came back out of order — adding it stops with an explanation rather than building a broken article, and it does not use up one of your articles. A failure that cannot succeed on a second try no longer offers a Retry button.

entries.title: Article images come from our copies
entries.body: Where we have already stored an article's images, the article shows ours rather than fetching them from the publisher as you read. A figure that will not load leaves its caption behind rather than holding the whole article on a loading screen, and moving between articles no longer blanks the images. An article's export now counts its images correctly.

entries.title: More room for the article on smaller screens
entries.body: A mode's panel sits beside the article on a larger phone held sideways or a tablet upright, rather than covering it. The controls bar hides as you scroll, on every screen. The strip showing where you are shades the section you are in as well as the part, and a Search mark at the very end is no longer clipped.

entries.title: A new Structure view, and outlined quotes
entries.body: Structure is a new way to see an article: its parts on one side, the sections inside the part you are in on the other. Turn it on with the Experimental features switch on your profile page. In Quotes, marked lines are drawn with an outline rather than a fill, so quotes and Search hits no longer look alike.

entries.title: Your library, the public library, and What's new
entries.body: The library table no longer overlaps its heading row, and a long library shows a first page with a Show all button. The public library says what republishing an article means, with a page explaining what we do if you are the author. A What's new link in the footer lists what changed in each release.

entries.title: Dictation hears the article's own words
entries.body: When you speak into a text box, the article's own words are sent as vocabulary, so names it used to mistype come back right. Where a recording is refused for good, there is no longer a Retry button to press. The privacy page now says which services handle a recording, in place of a promise we could not check.

entries.title: Headings return on Wikipedia-style articles
entries.body: On Wikipedia and pages built like it, nearly every section heading was thrown away as the article was added, leaving the levels of detail and the outline with almost nothing to work from. On one test article, 2 of its 56 headings survived; all 56 do now.

entries.title: Jump to any mode by typing
entries.body: Press Cmd-K (Ctrl-K on Windows) on an article in your own library, or use the new button on the bar, and type the first letters of a mode — Glossary, Quotes, Timeline — to open it. The list marks which modes start a paid AI run before you choose one, and a What's new row takes you to this page.

entries.title: The quiz adapts as you answer
entries.body: Answer a question well and the next one is harder; get one wrong and the next is easier. There is nothing to set and no difficulty shown — the quiz pitches itself at you as you answer. The mark you see beside your answer is unchanged.

entries.title: Debate shows how each reply was matched
entries.body: Debate's responses are one list rather than two, and each row says how it was matched: the page links to the article, quotes it, or only names it. Copies of the article are no longer offered as replies, and a control hides the rows matched on the weakest grounds, saying how many it hid.

entries.title: Pointing at a button explains what it does
entries.body: Each mode button on the bar describes what it gives you and how it works, and whether opening it starts a paid AI run. The Comments, Tweets and Metadata buttons carry the same cards. One of them told a reader looking at an article shared with them that comments belonged to whoever added it; it no longer does.

entries.title: Run an article's generated parts again
entries.body: The article's Metadata page offers a fresh run of nine things the app builds for a piece, among them its glossary, quotes, ideas, timeline and quiz. Each asks twice and says what it will cost before it starts, a failed run leaves the existing result in place, and a half-typed reading purpose is no longer wiped by the refresh.

entries.title: Escape closes one thing, and keeps your draft
entries.body: One press of Escape could close two overlapping things at once, and pointing at a term while writing a note could throw the note away. Escape closes only what you meant it to. Closing a chat, or Referee's How-this-works card, also puts the keyboard back on the button you opened it from rather than at the top of the page.

entries.title: Summary questions no longer restate the summary
entries.body: The question shown beside a section in Summary mode could simply restate that section's own summary line, or end up oddly punctuated. Both are fixed, and sections the app adds when it goes a level deeper come with a question of their own instead of a plain summary line.

entries.title: Notes and warnings survive from wiki pages
entries.body: Articles added from ArchWiki, and from documentation sites built with Docusaurus, lost the boxes marking a note, tip or warning: one kind went unrecognised, the other was dropped as navigation. Both are kept from now on. A separate fault that broke some paragraphs into pieces when an article was stored is also fixed.

entries.title: Delete an article for good
entries.body: Every article's Metadata page now has Delete permanently beneath Archive. It removes the article and everything built from or written on it, and asks you to confirm the article by name before it does. Archive still just puts something out of the way; this one cannot be undone, and it will not run while an article is still being added. The privacy page has been updated to match.

entries.title: Articles open before their paragraph labels finish
entries.body: A newly added article is ready to read before the short labels for each of its paragraphs have finished being written. The Paragraphs control tells you they are still arriving, and if they cannot be finished it says they are unavailable rather than leaving you waiting on something that will never come.

entries.title: The wordmark plays when you point at it
entries.body: Point at the Spideryarn name, or hold it on a touchscreen, and it plays one of thirteen short animations, chosen at random. The spider mark now sits beside the name on your library page as well, and the name is drawn in the same typeface everywhere it appears.

entries.title: Step rows show how long each step took
entries.body: On an article's Metadata page, the rows under What we did to it now tell you how long each step took as well as when it finished. Point at a row's time to see both.

entries.title: A proper foot to every page
entries.body: The footer is one hairline row: the wordmark and a line about the page on the left, links on the right. The Features page no longer ends twice, Pricing fills the width it has, and the short pages no longer trail off into empty space. Two of the bottom bar's tooltips became hover cards, and say less than they claimed.

entries.title: The empty strip at the top is gone
entries.body: On your own article, an empty black strip could sit across the top of the screen with nothing in it. That row is drawn only when it has something to show. Separately, when a comment fails to save, retry or delete, the Comments button turns red and the drawer shows what went wrong.

entries.title: Uploaded pages and repeated pastes are accepted
entries.body: A web page saved to your computer and then uploaded could be turned away as not a web page at all; those files are accepted now. And pasting a link you were already adding could be told the article had gone, when it had in fact just finished; that paste finds it instead.

entries.title: Buttons and text boxes work properly on touch
entries.body: On a phone or tablet, the ordering buttons in the Glossary and Quotes panels were too small to hit, and tapping a text box — a comment, a chat message, the feedback form — zoomed the page in and left it there. The buttons are a comfortable size, and typing no longer moves the zoom.

entries.title: Quotes stay marked in every mode
entries.body: The lines Quotes picks out as worth keeping are marked in the article itself whichever mode you have open, not only while Quotes is showing. On a touch screen, tapping a marked line still selects its paragraph, just as tapping any other line does.

entries.title: A new page describes Spideryarn's open-source code
entries.body: A new Open source page, linked from the site footer and from this changelog, describes Spideryarn's public code, its MIT licence, its documentation, and how AI agents contribute to it. This changelog also has a contents list, and each release is numbered, opens and closes, and links to the code it was built from, with only the newest open to begin with.

entries.title: The Commands button sits beside the logo
entries.body: When you are reading signed in, the Commands button comes straight after the Spideryarn logo, and the list it opens has new rows for Metadata, Tweets, Comments, Library, Profile, the public library and Feedback.

entries.title: Adding an article accepts the right things
entries.body: Some addresses that were not web pages, such as data files, news feeds and images, could be added as articles, while some uploaded web pages were wrongly refused; both are fixed. When an uploaded file cannot become an article, the message is about the file, not an address it never had, and an image-only PDF gets its own explanation.

entries.title: Tables and figures no longer go missing
entries.body: Some articles lost whole data tables when added, and some correction notices were dropped; both are kept, unless that would lose some of the article's own text. A figure could also stay blank for the rest of a read if our copy failed to load; it falls back to the publisher's plain image instead.

entries.title: Debate labels sources by whether they agree
entries.body: Debate could mark an outside source as Critical when it supported the article: the AI was judging the source's own tone, not whether it agreed with the claim it was set against. It is now asked to judge that, and earlier results still display. Debate is behind the Experimental features switch on your profile.

entries.title: Fewer controls in the way on touch screens
entries.body: On a narrow screen, such as a phone held sideways, the bar of mode buttons stayed up whenever a mode was open; it hides as you scroll when the mode sits beside the article. On touch screens, paragraph icons show only on the one you tapped, and tapping a link or picture no longer selects the paragraph beneath.

entries.title: The Feedback button sits with your library's controls
entries.body: On your library, the Feedback button sat in the corner of the window; it is now beside Profile at the top of the page. On an installed iPhone, the library's top row also clears the notch, and on touch screens its buttons are taller.

entries.title: Dictation drops an extra microphone request on Safari
entries.body: On Safari, and in the Spideryarn app added to an iPhone home screen, pressing the microphone button on a text box such as chat, comments or a quiz answer could ask for microphone permission twice. The app made an unnecessary first request before dictating, and it no longer does, which should leave you with one prompt. Dictation otherwise works as it did.

entries.title: Find more quotes without losing existing ones
entries.body: The Quotes panel now offers Find more, which adds fresh quotes to the list and keeps the ones already there, up to 120 in all. Quotes are outlined in the article faintly or strongly depending on how much they matter, and a chosen line now starts where a sentence starts rather than partway through it.

entries.title: Glossary answers appear as they are written
entries.body: Answers arrive word by word, both for a term you type in and for the Check the web action on an entry. An answer that is cut off is labelled unfinished rather than kept as if it were complete. If a term isn't in the article, Ask in chat opens a new conversation with the question already typed.

entries.title: Outline has been folded into Structure
entries.body: Structure shows its two linked columns when there is room beside the article, and a nested list of headings when there isn't, so a narrow panel no longer stacks the columns one above the other. In the list, a heading wraps onto a second line instead of being cut off. Old Outline links open Structure.

entries.title: Figures come through at a larger size
entries.body: Where a page offers an image at several sizes, we now take a larger one instead of whichever the page happened to name first. Diagrams and charts that were too small to read when you enlarged them come through legibly. This applies to figures gathered from now on, so articles you already have are unchanged.

entries.title: Press G to open a term's glossary entry
entries.body: From a link in the article, or from the paragraph you are on, pressing G opens one of that paragraph's underlined terms in Glossary without moving the page. Press G again to step through the paragraph's other terms, and Escape to return to where you were.

entries.title: A failing panel no longer breaks the article
entries.body: When a panel beside the article — Quotes, Glossary, Search, Timeline and the rest — hit an error, the whole reading view went with it. Only that panel is replaced now, with a message naming it; the article, the strip showing where you are, and the controls stay where they were.

entries.title: A new saved search or comment isn't lost
entries.body: Adding a saved search, a referee criterion or a comment while the panel was still loading could wipe what you had just added. Those panels now wait for the list before accepting a new entry, and a warning that your earlier items failed to load stays up instead of vanishing when you add one.

entries.title: A paragraph's link icon brightens on hover
entries.body: Pointing straight at the link icon next to a paragraph left it dimmed, while the icons beside it lifted as usual. It brightens like the others now.

entries.title: Citations: see the works an article cites
entries.body: A new Citations panel lists the works it finds a piece citing, ranked by how relevant and influential each one looks, with a sentence on why it matters and a jump to where the article first cites it. Where the article gave a link, DOI or arXiv identifier, it is there; where it gave none, you can ask for a search that only keeps a page it actually found. Turn on Experimental features on your profile page to see it, on articles you added.

entries.title: Quotes avoids repeating the same point
entries.body: When Spideryarn picks out the lines worth keeping from an article, each quote should say something the others do not, instead of several restating the piece's central point in different words. Asking for more quotes follows the same rule.

entries.title: Find it has limits and describes itself accurately
entries.body: Find it, in the Citations panel, could be pressed any number of times. It allows two searches at once, 20 an hour and 60 a day, and a press beyond that is refused before any search starts. Its description no longer promises exactly one web search. Citations is behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: Find it no longer replaces the article's link
entries.body: In Citations, if the list of works was rebuilt while Find it was still searching, the search result could replace a link the article itself gives, such as a DOI or arXiv address, until you reloaded the page. The article's own link is kept.

entries.title: Repeated citations no longer crowd out other works
entries.body: In Citations, one work listed several times could use up room in the list and push other works out. Repeats are merged before the list is cut to size, so each place holds a different work.

entries.title: Formulas display as maths; more PDF figures appear
entries.body: Where equations in an article are written out as TeX code, they are drawn as proper mathematics as you read, and quoting, comments, Chat, Search, Ideas, Timeline and Referee all work on passages that contain a formula. Some PDF figures drawn from lines and text rather than a picture, which used to show only their caption, appear as images.

entries.title: Paragraphs can be bookmarked with one press
entries.body: On your own articles, a paragraph with no comment on it has a bookmark button among the controls beside it. One press saves it, and it shows in the Questions drawer and the comment window as “Whole paragraph —” followed by its opening words. Before, bookmarking meant selecting text and saving an empty comment. A short paragraph's controls also no longer show a second, unexplained “…” button at the foot.

entries.title: Chat is asked to look beyond the article
entries.body: When you ask where a passage, work or author stands in the wider debate, Chat is instructed to search the web and say where each claim came from; this is guidance, not a guarantee. Web links are labelled “From the web”. Chat, Remember and live conversation can also read the list of works the article cites, when there is one.

entries.title: Quotes can run to a whole paragraph
entries.body: Quotes can run to several sentences or a whole paragraph, up to 1,200 characters rather than 400, so a quote makes sense out of context. The “Use your profile” tick-box is gone: new glossaries, quotes, ideas and chats use your reader profile whenever you have one.

entries.title: Hierarchy moves behind Experimental features
entries.body: Hierarchy is one of the experimental features: unless the Experimental features switch on your profile page is on, it is no longer offered among the modes you can pick. Structure, the view of how the article is organised, stays available to everyone.

entries.title: Feedback reports can include the article
entries.body: Feedback sent from your own article, with extra diagnostics chosen, may include the file it was made from and our copy of its text, within size limits; your notes, comments, chats and profile are not gathered with it, though a screenshot you add yourself shows whatever is on screen. Two reports sent at the same moment could have one reader's message or attachments filed with the other's; they cannot now.

entries.title: Fewer background checks, and dictation and tap fixes
entries.body: Your open article no longer checks for updates every eight seconds when nothing is running, which could use battery. Dictation on iPad now asks for a smaller recording, so it should no longer stop at its length limit after about 87 seconds. Rotating a zoomed-in iPad no longer leaves too few columns, and a first tap on a link or footnote marker opens its card instead of leaving the app.

entries.title: Stalled live conversations and cut-off answers are fixed
entries.body: A live conversation could sit on “Listening” or “Thinking” with no explanation. It now says when the microphone is muted, the connection drops or no reply comes, and offers Reconnect, or Enable sound if your device paused playback. The Live button no longer says “Resume” on a chat you only typed in, and Chat answers are no longer cut short.

entries.title: Choosing a mode tells you what it does
entries.body: When you pick a mode from the bar at the bottom of the article or from the command bar, its name and a sentence about what it does appear over the panel for three seconds, then fade. This helps most on a tablet or phone, where the bar has no room to spell out the mode's name. It does not appear for Plain or Hierarchy, or when you arrive by a link, Back or a reload, and it goes away as soon as you tap or start typing.

entries.title: Search, Glossary, Quotes and Citations show more at first
entries.body: Search by meaning opens with its results in priority order, and the Search, Glossary, Quotes and Citations panels start with their bar set lower. Most of each list is showing when the panel opens, so you no longer have to drag the bar down to see it.

entries.title: Asking about a passage starts with a simpler question
entries.body: Pressing ? beside a passage puts "Help me understand." into the chat in your name, in place of a longer two-part question. The AI still knows to look beyond the passage itself: around it, earlier in the article, or at context the article leaves unstated.

entries.title: Every page footer links to shared articles
entries.body: The footer at the bottom of the site's pages has a Shared articles link, next to Features, to the public library of articles readers have shared. The command bar uses the same name for that page, where it used to say Public shelf.

entries.title: The way back to your place survives changing modes
entries.body: After following a link within an article, the control that takes you back used to vanish if you then changed mode, columns or sort order. It stays now, and takes you back past those changes. Turning your phone or tablet no longer loses your place in the article, and very long articles do less needless redrawing along the way.

entries.title: Library actions are reachable on touchscreens
entries.body: On a tablet or touchscreen laptop, the actions for each article in your library were hidden and hard to find. Each article has a finger-sized ⋯ menu that lists its actions in words, and a second tap closes it. The pencil for renaming your own articles stays visible on those devices too.

entries.title: Search results jump without covering the passage
entries.body: Clicking or tapping a search result opened the card explaining its score over the very passage you had just jumped to, and on touch it stayed open. Tapping a result's words now just takes you to the passage; the card opens only from the dot, score and bar beside it.

entries.title: Tweets starts writing however you arrive
entries.body: Opening Tweets on one of your articles with no thread yet only started writing one if you pressed the mode; arriving by a link, a reload or Back showed an empty page and a button. It starts writing the thread whichever way you arrive.

entries.title: Citations are marked in the article text
entries.body: Once an article's citations have been found, its owner sees up to three mentions of each cited work, and its reference entry, underlined with a dashed line wherever the app can place them exactly. Point at or tap one to see the work, its authors and year, why the article uses it, and a link to it or a Google Scholar search. Looking a work up on the web still happens in the Citations panel.

entries.title: The Find it button explains what it does
entries.body: In the Citations panel, pointing at or tapping Find it on a work that only has a Scholar search shows a card saying that it runs a paid web search, and what happens if it finds the work or does not. Before, there was only a small browser tooltip, which never appeared on touch screens.

entries.title: Structure rows show more detail on hover
entries.body: When the Structure panel is wide enough to show two columns, pointing at a part or section row shows a card with what is not already on screen, such as its gist or the sections inside it. Rows with nothing more to add, and paragraph rows, have no card, and the cards need a mouse rather than a tap.

entries.title: FAQ mode answers questions with the article's own words
entries.body: A new FAQ mode lists the questions a careful reader might ask of your article, and under each shows passages from the article itself rather than a written answer. The quoted words are checked against the article; which passage answers which question is the AI's reading. It is offered when the Experimental features switch on your profile page is on.

entries.title: The article shows where you have spent time
entries.body: With the Experimental features switch on, the strip showing where you are in the article grows wider beside the parts you have spent time reading, and a faint line marks them next to each paragraph. Only time while the tab is open and you are active counts, and the privacy policy says these totals are kept.

entries.title: Feedback shows the reports you already sent
entries.body: The Feedback dialog has an Earlier tab beside Write, listing your own previous reports, newest first, with their dates and full text. You can check what you already told us before writing again.

entries.title: Equations are drawn as maths in more articles
entries.body: A newly added PDF keeps its equations as maths, and several common ways web pages write equations are turned into the same form, so they are drawn as maths in the article. A formula the app cannot draw is left as the page had it. Refreshing a web article with equations can make a paragraph containing maths count as a new passage, so a note or link attached to it may come loose.

entries.title: Error messages are written for readers
entries.body: When something went wrong in Chat, Glossary, Search, Referee, the quiz, a live conversation, your library or while adding an article, the message could show raw technical text. You see a plain sentence instead. On Safari, a lost connection shows the same message about not reaching the server as other browsers.

entries.title: PDF figures no longer sit under wrong captions
entries.body: In a PDF where a tall picture crossed a page break, a figure could show the previous figure's picture under its caption. The app checks that the caption belongs on that page before attaching a picture. A picture it cannot match stays missing rather than being shown in the wrong place.

entries.title: Adding an article survives a bad AI answer
entries.body: Adding a web page or PDF could fail at “Labelling the paragraphs” because of one malformed answer from the AI. The app asks again for the paragraphs it is missing, or redoes the batch, instead of stopping.

entries.title: An older Quotes list can be chosen again
entries.body: A Quotes list chosen some time ago could get stuck short, because Find more could not add to it. Such a list offers “Choose them again” instead. A quote picked again in the same words from the same paragraph keeps its link.

entries.title: On iPad, the first tap shows the card
entries.body: On iPad, tapping a dot on the strip showing where you are in the article jumped straight to that place. The first tap opens the dot's card; a second tap on the open card jumps.

entries.title: Outlines and glossaries explain jargon in plain words
entries.body: The short summaries and questions in Hierarchy and Outline, and the Glossary's definitions, are written for a reader outside the field: a technical term can stay, but the sentence around it must make sense without it. Older glossaries are marked as from a different version and can be regenerated; a hierarchy shows the new wording when it is made again.

entries.title: Filter your library by topic
entries.body: Your library now shows a row of topic chips drawn from the articles you have added. Click one, or several, to narrow the list; topics combine with the search box and the Unread chip, and hold together. Archived articles, when they are shown, are narrowed the same way and stay visible while you search.

entries.title: Trajectory mode walks you through an article
entries.body: Trajectory turns the lines worth keeping in an article into a route you can step through — with the panel, the arrow keys, or a door in the text just after the passage you are on — at three levels of depth. Each stop says what to look for, and gathers what the other panels already hold about that passage: its terms, the ideas it assumes, questions and dates. It is there for articles you added, with the Experimental features switch turned on.

entries.title: The library's table view shows more
entries.body: Long titles and source lines wrap in full, and pointing at a title opens a card with the gist, when you added and last opened it, how long it is and who can see it. You can hide columns from a Columns menu, and the table no longer shifts the page sideways on a phone.

entries.title: Passage links show a preview before you jump
entries.body: Point at a link to a passage and a card shows its section and a preview of the text, instead of a plain tooltip. Follow one and the paragraph flashes once the page settles. A link whose passage is no longer in this version of the article says so, rather than going nowhere.

entries.title: Structure shows two columns only when they fit
entries.body: Structure's two-column face now appears only when the window is wide enough to keep both columns readable; narrower windows show the single list instead. Separately, the card naming a mode when you switch to it now sits at the foot of the panel rather than over the first controls or results.

entries.title: Start an article again from scratch
entries.body: For articles you added, with the Experimental features switch on, an article's Metadata page has a Start this article again control. It re-reads the copy we hold and rebuilds what was made from it, after a confirmation spelling out what is kept, what is lost and what it costs, and it shows progress while it runs.

entries.title: Figures from PDFs land in the right place
entries.body: When an article comes from a PDF, a figure whose picture could not be matched to its caption was sometimes left out or paired with the wrong image. The app now looks again at that page and the ones either side, and places a picture only when there is a single clear candidate.

entries.title: Papers with many authors keep all of them
entries.body: An article from a journal or preprint site could arrive with a single name on its byline, even when the paper listed many more. Adding an article now reads the full author list the publisher provides, so the byline matches the paper.

entries.title: Trajectory no longer needs the Experimental switch
entries.body: Trajectory, which takes you through an article's quotes as a route of stops, is now there for every article you added, without turning on Experimental features; visitors still see only a note explaining it. Each step briefly highlights the passage you land on, each stop shows where it sits in the article, and Plan it again builds a fresh route. Quotes and Trajectory now sit right after Summary.

entries.title: What the AI writes uses plainer words
entries.body: Summaries, glossary entries, answers in Chat and about a passage, and the other text the AI writes for an article are now asked to use ordinary words while keeping exactly the same meaning. In side-by-side reads, the plainer versions read better. Existing Glossary, Ideas, Quotes, Timeline, Quiz, FAQ, Debate, Citations and Trajectory results now say they were made the older way, and offer the usual way to make them again.

entries.title: Library topics cover more of your articles
entries.body: The topic labels above your library are now picked so the first few cover more articles and overlap less, and near-twins like AI and AIs become one. Each label has a coloured dot showing its rank, All topics opens the full set in place, and a detail view shows each topic's counts and a few of its articles.

entries.title: Referee's Claims check works on long papers
entries.body: On long papers, the Claims check in Referee could spend its whole allowance thinking and show nothing. Claims and Criteria now keep room for the answer. If any AI answer runs out of room this way, the message now says the limit was on our side and offers a retry, instead of blaming the article.

entries.title: Answers stop naming passages by internal codes
entries.body: Answers sometimes pointed to a passage by a reference number or code that appears nowhere on screen. Chat, Search, Ideas, FAQ, Quiz, Citations, Timeline, Referee and the other modes that refer to passages are now told not to. It should happen much less, though an answer that still does is not corrected.

entries.title: Referee keeps true notes of a paper's limits
entries.body: Referee's Claims check could hide an accurate restatement of a paper's own limitation just because it contained wording like "no transfer experiments were performed". It now keeps them.

entries.title: Trajectory's route covers more of the Ideas
entries.body: Trajectory, which walks you through an article's quotes in rounds of increasing depth, plans its route with the article's Ideas (the claims the piece rests on) and its sections in view. Each pass aims to cover as many of those Ideas as the quotes reach. If the Quotes, Ideas or outline change after a route is planned, it says so.

entries.title: Trajectory skips the Abstract and has larger arrows
entries.body: Trajectory's route no longer includes quotes from an article's Abstract or its opening summary, which are already a condensed place to get the gist. If an article has no usable quotes outside those, Trajectory tells you that. The arrows for the previous and next stop are larger.

entries.title: Jumping to a passage no longer overshoots
entries.body: Jumping to a passage, from a summary, a comment, the keyboard, a swipe or a Trajectory stop, could scroll past it when the page shifted during the move, cutting off its start. It lands on the passage now. Trajectory also flashes the quote's own words, not the whole paragraph, when you reach a stop or pick one from its list.

entries.title: Archived articles can be browsed with the rest
entries.body: The Show archived section at the foot of your library is gone. In its place is an Archived chip beside Unread, off to begin with: turn it on and archived articles join the one list, so sorting, search, Unread and the topics all apply to them. Archived articles are marked, and offer Put back instead of Archive. Topics that match nothing in the list you are looking at are no longer shown, apart from one you have chosen, so you can still remove it.

entries.title: Trajectory stops show the words of each quote
entries.body: Each stop in the Trajectory panel shows the quote, in quotation marks, rather than only the section it comes from. The current stop is shown in full, the others shortened; point at one, or reach it with the keyboard, to read the whole quote. A repeated section no longer shows a ditto mark that looked like a quotation mark.

entries.title: Trajectory keeps your place in view
entries.body: Switching to Trajectory takes you to its current stop, with a chip to take you back, and the stop list keeps the current one in view. The end of each pass offers one button, More detail; the note on where passages come from sits behind an info button. A jump to a passage lands it mid-screen, not at the top.

entries.title: The Glossary panel takes less room
entries.body: The Glossary panel is more compact, which helps on a phone: the Look up explanation moves into its button's tooltip, and the heading folds into the sort row. Labels such as person, place and work become icons you can point at. Notes on your reading profile say whether the text was written for your current profile or an older one.

entries.title: Library topics skip vague words used in passing
entries.body: The topics above your library are less often vague words, such as 'following' or 'process', that an article only used in passing. A vague word becomes a topic for an article only when the article uses it again and again, and two topics sharing a root word are less often placed side by side.

entries.title: The spider sits beside the Spideryarn name
entries.body: The spider mark appears next to the Spideryarn Reading name at the top and foot of every page, and plays its animations when you point at it or press and hold. The Beta badge moves to the right-hand side of the top bar, and pages that showed the logo twice show it once.

entries.title: Redoing the AI's work lives in one place
entries.body: On an article's Metadata page, the controls for having the AI redo its work are one section, Re-run AI processing, folded shut above Archive, with Trajectory added. The redo buttons inside Trajectory, Ideas, Timeline, Debate, Quiz and Tweets are gone; a panel that is out of date still offers its fix, and each still shows a redo's progress or failure.

entries.title: Diagram moves behind the Experimental features switch
entries.body: Diagram is now one of the experimental modes, so it is normally left off the mode buttons unless the Experimental features switch on your profile page is on. If you are already in Diagram, it stays visible. The features page marks it as experimental.

entries.title: Mode buttons are grouped; Experimental is a switch
entries.body: The row of mode buttons is reordered into six groups, with a thin line between each. The Experimental button is drawn as an on/off switch and says whether pressing it will turn experimental features on or off, so it reads as a setting rather than one more mode.

entries.title: Bigger paragraph icons; the grey line explains itself
entries.body: The small icons beside each paragraph are a little bigger. Point at the thin grey line beside a paragraph and a note says what it is: it gets darker the longer you spend reading there, and only you see it.

entries.title: The privacy page covers everything the AI does
entries.body: The privacy and features pages cover everything the AI prepares or writes, not three named features, and the privacy page says each may send the AI service the article, your question, a quiz answer or your profile. The public-sharing explanation says its quotes are the author's own words, picked out by the AI. What we promise has not changed.

entries.title: Articles show their authors and where they work
entries.body: Newly added articles can show their authors' names and the institutions they belong to, at the top of the article and on its Metadata page. Each name links to a search of your library for that author, and each institution opens a small card. For PDFs, the names the AI finds are checked against the page before they are kept. Visitors to a public article do not see them, and articles already in your library are unchanged until the app reads them again from the original.

entries.title: Hierarchy mode has been removed
entries.body: The Hierarchy mode, which showed the article compressed into columns beside the text, has been removed; old links to it open Structure instead. Section titles in Structure, Summary and Diagram no longer show the article's own number beside the one Spideryarn adds, so each section is numbered once. And after the sections are laid out afresh, Structure's marker of where you are moves back to the first section when that is where you are, rather than staying on a later one.

entries.title: Independent modes are built at the same time
entries.body: When more than one mode is being prepared for an article, those that do not use each other's results are built at the same time rather than one after another. Trajectory still waits while Quotes or Ideas is being built, and Illustrated waits for Sketch, because each uses what the other makes.

entries.title: The AI helps pick your library's topics
entries.body: The topics above your library are still found by the app itself, but the AI now rates each one and the pick is made from those ratings. Your library opens with its existing list at once; if anything the ratings rely on has changed, a refreshed choice arrives shortly after. The privacy policy says what the AI is given.

entries.title: No more notices about older AI instructions
entries.body: Trajectory, Ideas, Timeline, Debate, Quiz, Quotes, Glossary, Citations and FAQ no longer show a notice, with a redo button, saying a result was made with an older version of the AI's instructions. Warnings that the article or your profile has changed still appear. FAQ and Citations can also be made again from the re-run section of the article's Metadata page.

entries.title: Back links are small icons
entries.body: The word "Back" at the top of pages is replaced by an arrow, or by a house for Home on the pages that describe Spideryarn, and pointing at it shows a label. The animated Spideryarn logo from the Contact page also appears at the top and bottom of those pages.

entries.title: Visitors can see more of a public article
entries.body: People reading a public article without signing in can see its Trajectory, FAQ, Citations and Debate, when those have already been made; before, Trajectory told them it was only for whoever added the article. Some links, and details of how each result was made, are held back, and the privacy policy says what is shared.

entries.title: Titles no longer show stray formatting tags
entries.body: A source in Debate could show its title with bits of web-page formatting left in, such as "<i>". Titles from web searches, link previews, Referee's citations, the Citations mode and newly added articles are saved as plain text. Titles saved before this change may still show them.

entries.title: Trajectory stops show ideas and questions in place
entries.body: In Trajectory, a stop's ideas open right on the card, one at a time, showing what each one says, and the FAQ question for a stop appears above its quote, with the passages that answer it a click away. Each stop has a small outline showing where it sits in the article, a little drawing of the route replaces 'Stop k of N', and the links to Glossary, Ideas and FAQ are icons, so you can reach them without leaving Trajectory.

entries.title: Trajectory's deeper passes no longer repeat stops
entries.body: In Trajectory, the More and Most passes each walk only their own stops, rather than taking you back through the ones you already read at Gist. Switching pass takes you to its first stop and each pass shows its own count; at Most, the note on how much you have covered counts the stops from all three passes.

entries.title: The modes along the bottom are regrouped
entries.body: Glossary, Ideas and Timeline sit in the same group as Trajectory, Quotes and FAQ, and Search has moved to sit with Chat and Remember. The bar reads: Plain | Structure, Summary, Diagram | Trajectory, Quotes, FAQ, Glossary, Ideas, Timeline | Referee, Citations, Debate | Search, Chat, Remember.

entries.title: Long dictations keep going, and keep the audio
entries.body: Dictation no longer cuts off partway through a long recording: it sends what you say in parts while you keep talking, and gives you the whole text when you stop. Your recording is also kept on this device until its words arrive, so if the page closes, reloads or crashes, the next time you open the same box you are offered the audio to save or try again. Signing out deletes those copies, and any left behind are cleared after a week.

entries.title: Uploaded papers get a guessed source link
entries.body: When you open a paper you uploaded without a web address, the app searches for the paper's page online. It shows a link only when that page matches closely — its title, its first author where known, and either a matching DOI or arXiv number or its opening text — drawn dim with a question mark, at the top of the article and on its Metadata page. If nothing is certain enough, Metadata says so. Only you see the guess.

entries.title: Citations say what was read, and can check it
entries.body: Citations panel entries say their sentence is what the article uses the work for, and that the work itself has not been read. Look it up, replacing Find it, searches for the work and has the AI judge whether the snippet the search returns supports that use, quoting only words really in it. It is behind the Experimental features switch.

entries.title: FAQ and Debate can list the central items first
entries.body: In new FAQs, the AI rates each question for how central and how hard it is, and the central, approachable ones come first; a slider sets how many show, or switch to reading order. Debate rows lead with the found work's title, detail behind More, and new debates can be prioritised too. Older lists keep their order until made again.

entries.title: Tweets opens beside the article like other modes
entries.body: The Tweets thread opens in the panel beside the article like any other mode, not on a page of its own, and old links to that page still work. In newly made threads, a post can link to the passages it came from; follow one to jump to it in the article. Older threads stay unlinked until made again.

entries.title: On a phone, passage links show the passage
entries.body: On a narrow screen, where a panel covers the article, following a link to a passage from any mode hides the panel so you can see the passage. A small back button, naming the mode, brings the panel back just as you left it.

entries.title: Keyboard shortcuts for the library and Chat
entries.body: On a computer, your library's search box is ready to type in when the page opens, and Cmd-Enter (Ctrl-Enter) in an article opens its Metadata page. In Chat, Enter no longer sends a half-written question while you are picking characters in Japanese or Chinese input, and the Send button shows its shortcuts when you point at it.

entries.title: Sending feedback closes the window straight away
entries.body: After you send feedback, its window closes at once and a short thank-you appears in the corner, going away by itself after a few seconds. Pointing at it keeps it on screen.

entries.title: Investigate a cited work from Citations
entries.body: Articles you added have an Investigate button beside each work in Citations: it searches the web for that work and writes how it bears on the article, and the answer is saved for later. Quotations it gives are checked word for word against the article, the reference or passages Look it up confirmed, and an answer that fails is stopped and not kept. On a touch screen, the first tap on Investigate or Look it up shows what it costs, and a second runs it.

entries.title: The library's Spideryarn heading plays its animations
entries.body: Pointing at or tapping the Spideryarn heading at the top of your library plays one of the logo's animations, picked at random. Before, only the spider could move; the letters join in as well, with their movements sized to the larger heading.

entries.title: ⌘-K opens the command bar on Metadata
entries.body: On the Metadata page of an article you added, ⌘-K or Ctrl-K and the Commands button did nothing; both open the command bar there. Choosing a mode from it takes you to that mode without starting any paid AI work.

entries.title: A new article can arrive with its modes ready
entries.body: While an article is being added, a checkbox offers to build its main modes, such as Glossary, Quotes and Ideas, as soon as it is in, before the article opens. It is ticked by default and your browser remembers your choice. It saves opening a new paper and then waiting for each mode in turn; the checkbox says plainly that this uses paid AI calls.

entries.title: Citations link to copies already in Spideryarn
entries.body: In the Citations panel of an article you own, a cited work that is also an article you can open here now links straight to it, marked as in your library or in the public library. Works are matched by DOI, arXiv number or web address, or by title only when enough of it agrees and the first author does not conflict. You can go from a reference to the piece itself without searching for it.

entries.title: Library topics are coloured by what they share
entries.body: The topics shown above your library now take their colour from the articles they have in common: topics covering many of the same articles get neighbouring colours, and a topic that shares nothing gets a colour of its own. Before, the colour only followed a topic's place in the list, so it told you nothing.

entries.title: The quiz builds step by step toward the takeaways
entries.body: The quiz is now an ordered path of up to 20 small questions, where it used to be 12, each answerable in a sentence or two and leading gradually to the article's key takeaways. Most questions start by recapping the answer before; that recap is hidden when you have just answered correctly and moved straight on. Any quiz written before this change is now out of date, and long papers have more time for theirs to be written.

entries.title: FAQ questions can be sorted by centrality or difficulty
entries.body: The FAQ panel adds two orders, most central and hardest, beside prioritised and reading order; they list every question, with any that lack a score at the end. The note about where the answers come from has moved out of the foot of the panel into an (i) at the end of the order row.

entries.title: Investigating a citation checks the web first
entries.body: In the Citations panel, the separate Look it up button is gone. Pressing Investigate on a cited work now first searches the web for it, shows what it found, then writes its longer reading against that page, so the reading rests on the checked source. The reading also has more room to finish.

entries.title: Uploaded articles can be rebuilt from their stored copy
entries.body: In your library, the rebuild action used to be greyed out for articles with no web address, such as uploads. It now works for them, reprocessing the copy we already keep instead of fetching again. It stays unavailable only when no reusable stored copy exists, and its label says so.

entries.title: Spoken conversations in Remember no longer vanish
entries.body: A live spoken conversation started in Remember was saved as an ordinary chat, so returning to Remember opened a fresh, empty conversation and yours seemed to disappear. It is now kept as a Remember conversation, titled Remembering even if its first turn could not be transcribed.

entries.title: Library search finds text in archived articles
entries.body: Searching your library never found text inside archived articles, even with archived articles shown. With the chip, renamed Include archived, switched on, the search now covers them and marks passages that come from one. An older failed search can also no longer replace newer results.

entries.title: Say why you are reading while it loads
entries.body: While an article is being added, an optional box asks "Why are you reading this?" Your answer is saved before the app builds the rest of the article, so it reaches everything built for it. On your own articles, Trajectory shows "Reading for:" above its route, with a link to change it; with no reason given, it offers a box to write one and plan the route for it. And Retry after a failed import opens the article once the retry works.

entries.title: The quiz can keep to what you read
entries.body: With reading time switched on, the quiz in Remember has an "Only what I've read" tick-box, ticked to start with. It asks only about passages you have spent enough time on, counts its questions within that set, and tells you roughly how much of the article you have read. If your reading history cannot be loaded, it shows every question and says why.

entries.title: Your questions appear in the Comments list
entries.body: Questions you asked about a passage, with the question button beside it or Chat about this, now sit in the Comments list with your comments, in the article's order and labelled Question. Press one to reopen its conversation, so an answer you closed is easy to find again.

entries.title: Run several searches at once in Search
entries.body: In Search, the Find button stays available while a search by meaning is running, so you can start several side by side. Only asking the very same question again while it is still running is refused, with a note saying why.

entries.title: Re-running one panel no longer asks first
entries.body: On an article's Metadata page, Run and Run it again start straight away. Start again, which redoes the whole article, still asks first and has moved to the top of the list. Sketch, Debate, Trajectory and Glossary show a short note on cost or what a re-run does, and a quick second press of Run or Retry is ignored.

entries.title: Filter your earlier feedback by shipped or not
entries.body: The Earlier tab of the Feedback window has All, Shipped and Not shipped filters, and reports whose change has gone live are marked Shipped. You can see at a glance what came of what you told us.

entries.title: PDF paragraphs no longer break at page turns
entries.body: A PDF paragraph running across a page turn, or past a figure or table, could be split in two, stranding half a sentence. It is joined up, figure captions that continue are kept whole, and author names no longer carry footnote numbers and asterisks once the names check out. This applies to PDFs added or processed again from here on.

entries.title: Figures kept in more web articles
entries.body: Some web articles, including Springer Nature pages and some Substack-style posts, lost their figures when added. They are kept, unless keeping them would cost some of the article's own text, and the "Full size image" button beside Springer Nature figures is left out. This applies to articles added, or processed again, from now on.

entries.title: Phrases that point elsewhere in the article link there
entries.body: In articles you have added, a phrase that refers to a passage developed elsewhere in the piece is underlined with dots. Point at it to see a card for that passage; click, tap or press Enter to jump to it. You can follow a claim to the passage that backs it up without losing your place hunting for it.

entries.title: Illustrated diagrams can use the paper's own figures
entries.body: For a PDF paper whose figures the app has kept, the Illustrated diagram is given those figures to work from, so the picture it draws can include the paper's own charts and images. Articles without figures are drawn as before. Diagram is behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: Chat and glossary look-ups give shorter answers
entries.body: Chat answers aim for one or two short paragraphs, usually under 300 words unless you ask for more. Looking up a term in the Glossary, or checking it on the web, gives one or two short paragraphs and never more than three.

entries.title: Arrow keys step through the Remember quiz
entries.body: In the quiz half of Remember, the left and right arrow keys move to the previous or next question, and the step buttons are icons that name their keys when you point at them. The keys do nothing while you have a typed answer not yet marked, or while dictation is on, so a stray press cannot lose your words.

entries.title: Trajectory's controls fit on one row and name their keys
entries.body: In a narrow Trajectory panel, the (i) button no longer drops onto a line of its own below the depth buttons. The previous and next arrows, and the Next stop button, show a card when you point at them saying you can press the left and right arrow keys while reading.

entries.title: The Tweets panel keeps a steadier width
entries.body: The Tweets panel takes a fixed share of the room beside the article, so on an iPad it no longer swings from narrow to very wide when you turn it. Its copy buttons, for the whole thread and for each post, are icons that explain themselves when you point at them, and are larger to tap.

entries.title: Summary mode has a plain-words Simple view
entries.body: Summary mode has a new switch between Gists and Simple. Simple gives a few short paragraphs about the piece in everyday words, each linked to the passages it draws on, with a note that the AI wrote them. They are written the first time you press Simple and kept for next time. If you make an article public, visitors can read its Simple summary too, and the privacy page says so.

entries.title: Quiz questions appear in the article itself
entries.body: In your own articles, once a quiz has been made, each question shows as a quiet line in the text, in every mode, just after the passage its answer draws on; in Trajectory it sits between a stop's passage and Next stop. Press one to open the quiz at that question. Only the question is shown, never anything that would give away an earlier answer. When a quiz is made again, the old ticks no longer carry over to the new questions.

entries.title: The quiz points you back to sections
entries.body: After you get a quiz answer wrong, a Where to look again list appears beneath it, naming up to three sections where your wrong answers came from, most-missed first. Press a name to jump there, or return to the first question you missed in it. It names places only, never a score, and nothing is kept or sent.

entries.title: Citations name the words that cite each work
entries.body: Each Citations row shows the words the article first used to cite the work, and jumping lands on that citation, not the whole paragraph. In your own PDFs, numbered citations are matched to the reference list, so rows show the real authors and year rather than invented titles, with the full entry when you point at it.

entries.title: Archive and Share sit at the top
entries.body: Archive and Share… are just under the title on an article's Metadata page. Share… takes you to the sharing settings; it does not publish anything by itself. The Authors, Export and Delete sections start folded away.

entries.title: Release dates here say how long ago
entries.body: Each release on this page says how long ago it went out, in its heading and in the list of contents, and keeps up to date while the page is open. Point at one to see the exact time; older releases show their date instead.

entries.title: The privacy page names our email service
entries.body: The privacy page lists the service that sends the app's account emails among the companies that handle data for us. It was already sending those emails; it was missing from the list.

entries.title: Debate picks out the threads across its sources
entries.body: When Debate gathers the sources that respond to an article, it now also picks out the themes that several different works share, and stars the key sources with a line on why each matters. Choose a thread to see only the sources on it, with the counts following your choice. It applies to Debates made or remade on your own articles.

entries.title: Quizzes follow why you said you are reading
entries.body: If your profile says why you are reading, the quiz in Remember now asks mostly about the parts of the article that bear on that. Quizzes you already have stay as they are; the change applies to a quiz when it is made or remade.

entries.title: Library topics show that they are loading
entries.body: While the topics above your library are still being worked out, the row now shows "Loading topics…" instead of nothing, and on a longer library, faint outlines where the topics will go.

entries.title: PDF footnotes are kept in a Notes list
entries.body: Footnotes in a PDF used to be dropped when you added it, leaving bare numbers in the text with nothing behind them. They are now kept, in a Notes list at the end of the article. Where the app can tell which number in the text a note belongs to, pointing at that number shows the note, and the note links back to the passage. PDFs already in your library are unchanged.

entries.title: Privacy policy describes reading time more accurately
entries.body: The privacy policy's line about how long you spend on each part of an article now says that some of Spideryarn's features use those totals, to show you where you have been, for example. The old wording named only two places on the reading page and was no longer complete. The policy is dated 1 October 2026.

entries.title: Shipped feedback reports show as Shipped
entries.body: In the Feedback dialog's Earlier tab, some reports whose change had already shipped were shown as not shipped, and the Shipped and Not shipped filters put them in the wrong place. They now carry the Shipped badge and filter correctly.

entries.title: High-powered AI for any article you own
entries.body: You can switch on High-powered AI for an article you own, from its Metadata page, so the AI's work on that article uses a more capable AI. Switching it on takes a one-time extra charge from your article allowance, half as much while the article is public, and is refused if your allowance would not cover it. Switching it off does not give the charge back; switching it on again later for the same article is free.

entries.title: Summary in plain words at three levels
entries.body: Summary's controls fit on one row: Parts or Sections, and a slider for plain words with three levels, Brief, Simple and Fuller, in place of the single Simple button. One press writes all three. The paragraphs take account of what you have told us about yourself and your reading goal on your profile, marked with a 'written for you' badge, and a Write it again button appears if your profile has changed since.

entries.title: Investigate reads the cited paper itself
entries.body: When you investigate a cited work, the app tries to fetch the paper, has the AI pick up to three passages that bear on the claim, and keeps only quotations it finds word for word there. Each shows its page and how the AI judges it bears on the claim. When web search finds nothing, the paper alone can answer.

entries.title: PDF citations link to the paper itself
entries.body: In a PDF article's Citations list, a work whose reference gives a single DOI or arXiv number, the standard reference numbers for papers, links straight to it instead of a Google Scholar search. Citations and Debate may also fill in a missing author and year from public records of papers, when the title matches, and say where it came from.

entries.title: Public articles show Debate, citations and cross-links
entries.body: Visitors to a public article see its Debate (the summing-up, the threads, and how each key source bears on them), its citations where they match the article's own reference list, and links from a claim to the passage behind it. Some citation details read from a PDF stay visible only to the article's owner.

entries.title: More AI work runs at the same time
entries.body: Up to six pieces of AI work, such as adding an article or building a mode, can run at once, where it was three. Opening several modes on one article used to take every place, leaving other work waiting in line.

entries.title: Privacy page covers payments and sign-up emails
entries.body: The privacy page no longer says payments are not switched on. It says you enter card and billing details on Stripe's page and we do not keep them, and lists what we do keep. It also says that when you first sign up or upgrade, we email ourselves a note with your email address and account id.

entries.title: Articles can no longer fake the app's links
entries.body: Hidden formatting in an article's original page could make the reading view show a preview card, or a link to another passage, on words the app never linked. Formatting the app does not recognise is now removed, including from articles already in your library. Maths should look the same as before.

entries.title: Annotations: a column of notes beside the article
entries.body: A new Annotations mode, behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page, puts notes in a column to the right of the article: a question to think about beside the first full paragraph of each part, and a mark where each of the article's ideas first appears. A heading at the top shows which part and section you are in, with one sentence on the article's overall argument. On narrow windows the column is hidden.

entries.title: The command bar opens a mode's options directly
entries.body: The command bar lists each mode's options as well as the modes, such as Remember > Quiz, Diagram > Illustrated, Referee > Claims and Summary > Simple. Typing "quiz" or "illustrated diagram" and pressing Enter opens that mode with the option already chosen, just as if you had pressed its button.

entries.title: Quiz instructions take more account of your profile
entries.body: When your profile says something about you or why you are reading, the AI that writes your quiz is asked to let both shape which parts it covers, the kinds of question and how hard they are, and in a longer quiz to finish on the article's conclusion and its evidence. This applies when a quiz is made or remade.

entries.title: Trial typefaces show who wrote each passage
entries.body: With the Experimental features switch on, the article itself appears in a serif typeface, anything the AI wrote in Courier Prime, and anything you typed in Arial, so you can tell at a glance whose words you are reading. The rest of the app keeps its usual typeface.

entries.title: Long addresses and chat's Latest button on phones
entries.body: A long web address written out in an article's text, rather than as a link, could push the page sideways on a phone; it now wraps onto the next line. In Chat, the Latest button could cover the last line of the conversation; it now sits in its own row between the conversation and the box you type in.

entries.title: The line under an article's title fits on phones
entries.body: On a phone-width screen, the line of details under an article's title (who wrote it, how many sections it has and so on) could not break onto a second line, so it pushed the page wider than the screen and let it slide sideways. It now wraps between details, moving a whole detail down a line where needed.

entries.title: You can reset a forgotten password
entries.body: The email sign-in form has a 'forgot your password?' link that sends you a reset email. Following the link in it opens a page where you choose a new password, typed twice, instead of signing you straight in. If the link cannot be read, you see an error rather than being sent somewhere by guesswork.

entries.title: Your notes can stay open beside another mode
entries.body: Annotations is no longer one of the modes but a switch at the right end of the mode bar, so the column of your notes can sit beside Glossary, Summary or whichever panel you have open. On a narrower window the panel comes first, and a line says the notes need a wider window or the panel closed. Old links to Annotations open with the notes shown. Annotations is behind the Experimental features switch on your profile page.

entries.title: Plain-words summaries are checked against the article
entries.body: When you generate the plain-words levels in Summary, each paragraph is checked against the passages it cites. If one says the opposite of what its passage says, that level is written once more, which can add a little waiting. This catches slips such as borrowing the article's own term and getting it backwards.

entries.title: Citation cards say when a work is here
entries.body: In an article you own, pointing at a citation now shows whether the cited work is in your library or the public library, as the Citations panel already did. Your archived articles count, marked as archived, and an uploaded PDF can be matched to a citation by its DOI or arXiv number.

entries.title: The glossary button says what it will do
entries.body: On an article's Metadata page, the glossary button reads 'Find more terms' when it will add to the existing list. When it will write a new list instead, it says so, and says why: the article, the glossary's instructions or your profile has changed.

entries.title: Feedback is easier to find and tap
entries.body: The icons in the bar at the bottom of the reading view have more room, and Feedback sits at its right with a ring, so it looks different from the modes. Signed in, Feedback is in the top navigation on pages such as Features and Pricing, no longer covering a link. Earlier reports show the exact time and its age.

entries.title: Several searches at once no longer lose answers
